projects.title: Halo-lit reverse channel letter sign — parametric CAD + night-scene render
projects.summary: Exterior halo-lit sign for a street-front venue: 3D geometry, cut-ready DXF across a revision cycle, and a from-scratch night scene.

gallery.caption: Profile: reverse letters on standoffs, LED wash on the brick behind them.

gallery.caption: Macro detail of the halo spill on textured brick.

sections.problem: A street-front venue needed an exterior halo-lit sign, 2361 mm wide, with a specific lighting behaviour: the LED glow lands on the wall *behind* the letters, not on the letter faces. The client also went through a revision cycle after seeing the first render (decorative lines removed, text re-justified), so CAD, cut files and drawings had to stay in sync across versions.
sections.approach:
- Built the full 3D geometry parametrically: reverse channel letters with **100 mm** depth, **38 mm** standoff and a **50×30 mm** raceway.
- Iterated to v2 per client feedback and re-exported cut-ready **DXF** for both versions, plus a dimensioned technical PDF.
- Instead of a generic studio render, built a night scene from scratch in Blender (streetlight, wet pavement reflection, halo glow) and a 6-angle detail set for the presentation deck.
sections.result:
A client-facing presentation package — not just CAD files — that lets the business see the sign installed at night before committing to fabrication, reducing the risk of a costly post-install redesign.

> Client identity is withheld and lettering is blurred in these images while approval is pending.

sections.problem: A company needed its multi-part logo produced as a 3D wall sign for an office lobby — but only had a single reference render, no CAD source and no vector logo. The decision-maker also wanted to compare finishes in a realistic room, not on a blank studio wall.
sections.approach:
- Reverse-engineered the full piece geometry in FreeCAD from the reference image (1500 mm wide) and produced cut-ready DXF for every part plus a technical PDF with a standoff mounting plan (52 pins, ≥2 per piece).
- Wrote a scripted Blender scene (run headless from a shell batch) so camera, material and room are parameters: **7 angles × 2 finishes = 14 renders** at 2000 px, gold/brass vs. brushed stainless, ~2700 K warm halo, 20 mm standoff.
- Documented the open item (vector logo still needed from the client) instead of guessing and re-doing work later.
sections.result:
A QA-passed fabrication package ready the moment the vector logo arrives, and a 14-image comparison set where every frame shares the same geometry and light — so the finish decision is apples-to-apples.

> Client identity is withheld and the logo is blurred / cropped in these images while approval is pending.

projects.title: Hexagonal metal logo sign — halo-lit stainless, copper variant, raceway-free mounting
projects.summary: 1.2 m reception logo sign for an industrial company: brushed-stainless channel letters with cold-white halo, each piece on its own standoffs, rendered in stainless and copper.
projects.coverAlt: Office reception render with concrete wall, wood ceiling, desk and plants; the halo-lit logo sign is blurred pending client approval

gallery.alt: Wide reception render, logo blurred
gallery.caption: Reception scene — board-formed concrete, wood ceiling, cold-white halo. Logo blurred.

gallery.alt: Close-up of a brushed stainless letter stroke with standoff pin and halo glow
gallery.caption: Brushed stainless No.4 face and return, standoff pin and halo on concrete.

gallery.alt: Same close-up in a copper finish
gallery.caption: Same geometry and light in the copper variant (PVD-coated stainless suggested).

sections.problem: An industrial company wanted its hexagon logo built as a metal wall sign for the reception, about **1.2 m** wide, matching a reference render it had (brushed metal, cold-white halo, concrete wall). There was no vector logo — only that image — and the client asked for a copper option alongside stainless.
sections.approach:
- Redrew the logo from the reference as a parametric model: three large block letters filling a pointed hexagon (80 mm deep channel letters) and a two-word tagline running along the lower edges (40 mm deep), all faces in one plane. Overall **1200 × 1338 × 118 mm** off the wall.
- Halo-lit build: 3 mm brushed No.4 stainless faces, 1.2 mm stainless returns, 4.5 mm polycarbonate backs, 24 V halo LED modules (≈195 modules, ~140 W, 2 × 100 W PSUs).
- **No raceway**: every piece mounts on its own standoffs — 37 pins, at least 2 per piece and 3 on the large letters. Delivered a cut DXF (faces, backs, drill points), a 1:1 mounting-template DXF, a dimensioned technical PDF with BOM (~32 kg), plus STEP files for the fabricator on request.
- Rendered in a scripted Blender office scene: stainless × 3 views, copper × 2.
sections.result:
A QA-passed v1 package (all 19 cut contours checked against the CAD perimeters, every piece with ≥2 pins) now in client review. Render checks drove real design changes: the tagline at 70 mm cap height was unreadable on a 1.3 m logo, so it went to a condensed font at 125 mm; flat-cut tagline letters blended into the wall, so they became 40 mm channel letters with their own small halo. Open items are listed rather than guessed: the client's vector logo, wall type (concrete vs. drywall backing), finish choice and halo colour temperature.

> Client identity is withheld; the logo is blurred or cropped in these images while approval is pending.

projects.summary: Two-line non-illuminated channel-letter sign for a café façade: parametric letters on two raceway profiles, layered cut DXF, dimensioned drawing and warm wall-wash renders.

sections.problem: A café wanted its two-line name built as dimensional letters on the façade — **non-illuminated** (no light inside the letters), lit from outside by a wall-wash, with no backing panel: the letters had to sit on raceway profiles standing off the wall. The name contains a Turkish dotted capital **İ**, which generic sign templates and fonts routinely get wrong.
sections.approach:
- Generated the geometry parametrically in FreeCAD from the font outlines: 400 mm upper line, 200 mm lower line, **80 mm** letter depth, two aluminium raceways (128 / 90 mm high, 30 mm deep). Overall **1886 × 807 × 110 mm**.
- Materials specified for fabrication: 3 mm opaque cream acrylic faces, 1.27 mm dark-bronze aluminium returns, 2 mm aluminium raceway box profile, stainless fixings.
- Exported a **layered cut DXF** (CUT / ENGRAVE / RACEWAY, units in mm), one STEP/STL per letter, and a dimensioned technical PDF with a bill of materials (acrylic area, return-band length, estimated weight).
- Rendered the sign in Blender with a warm eave wall-wash from five angles for approval.
sections.result:
The client approved the renders; the fabrication files are ready and the package is waiting on a price quote. QA caught a real bug before anything left the studio: the first DXF had contour edges joined in the wrong order (zig-zag outlines, one perimeter measured 6305 mm instead of 2253 mm). The generator was fixed and v2 was verified by checking **contour area × 80 mm against the STL volume** for each letter, plus layer counts and drawing units.

> Client identity is withheld; the brand line is blurred or cropped out of these images, and only the generic lower line of the DXF is shown.

projects.title: Signage CAD → fabrication pipeline with QA gates
projects.summary: Scripted spec → CAD → DXF → PDF → render → package pipeline where every stage gates the next and a failed check stops the build.
projects.coverAlt: Diagram of the seven-stage signage pipeline from spec.json to client package

gallery.alt: Pipeline stage diagram
gallery.caption: Pipeline stages, each with its own QA gate.

gallery.alt: Macro render of a channel letter stroke and dot
gallery.caption: Render-stage output: channel-letter return depth, macro angle.

sections.problem: A fabrication-ready signage deliverable has four interdependent parts — 3D CAD geometry, CNC cut-ready DXF, a dimensioned technical PDF (BOM, mounting detail) and photoreal approval renders. Done by hand, every revision risks the DXF and PDF silently drifting out of sync with the CAD — a mistake that surfaces only when a fabricator is holding the wrong file.
sections.approach:
`spec.json` (dimensions, material, mount type) drives a staged build:

1. Parametric CAD generation (FreeCAD)
2. DXF export + contour QA
3. Technical drawing projection (TechDraw)
4. Dimensioned PDF + pagination QA
5. Multi-angle render batch + render sanity check (blank/overexposed frames caught via pixel std-dev)
6. Client package assembly + automated IP-leak check (fails if `.FCStd/.blend/.py/.json` sources would end up in the client zip)

Every stage writes to a single QA report; any failed check **stops** the build, so a partial package is never produced.
sections.result: From the project logs: ~1.5–2.5 h of active work per new design from spec (+30–40 min unattended render), and **0** CAD/DXF/PDF sync errors reaching a client package across completed projects. No time-savings percentage is claimed — there is no clean manual baseline to compare against.

projects.title: F1 Strategy Lab — does the undercut actually work?
projects.summary: 1070 first-stop pit pairs from the 2024 season: the earlier stopper came out ahead only 39.6% of the time.
projects.coverAlt: Bar chart: 424 of 1070 undercut attempts won (39.6%) versus a 50% coin-flip line

sections.problem: Broadcast commentary treats the undercut — pitting before your rival — as a near-guaranteed strategic win. Is it? The original plan was lap-by-lap telemetry via FastF1, but F1's live-timing backend started returning `403` without an authenticated F1 account mid-project.
sections.approach:
- Switched to the **Jolpica-F1 API** (community successor to Ergast): results, pit stops and lap-by-lap positions, all cached locally and rate-limited.
- Paired drivers who made their **first stop within 3 laps** of each other and checked who was ahead afterwards.
- Ran the full 2024 season: `python analysis/undercut_analysis.py --year 2024 --season --max-lap-gap 3`.
sections.result: **1070** pit-stop pairs analysed; the early stopper came out ahead in **424/1070 (39.6%)** — less than a coin flip. The same timing + position-tracking + win-rate technique transfers to any "does doing X earlier actually help?" business question (inventory timing, campaign timing).

projects.title: Vendor selection toolkit — AHP + TOPSIS
projects.summary: Auditable multi-criteria supplier ranking: AHP turns judgments into weights (with a consistency check), TOPSIS ranks the vendors.
projects.coverAlt: Charts of AHP criteria weights and TOPSIS closeness scores; the cheapest vendor ranks last

sections.problem: Small and mid-size businesses pick between 3–6 recurring suppliers on price, lead time, quality and reliability — usually with gut feel or weights invented in a spreadsheet minutes before the meeting, and no way to defend the choice later. In a signage business, choosing acrylic/metal material suppliers is exactly this problem.
sections.approach:
- **AHP** converts pairwise judgments ("how much more important is quality than price?") into criteria weights, with Saaty's **Consistency Ratio** flagging contradictory judgments.
- **TOPSIS** ranks vendors by distance to an ideal and a worst-case option under those weights.
- Packaged as a re-runnable CLI instead of a one-off spreadsheet.
sections.result: Worked example (`--example sign-materials`): weights Quality 0.466, Reliability 0.277, Price 0.161, Lead Time 0.096 with **CR = 0.011** (consistent). Ranking: QualityFirst Fab 0.718 → Acme Metals 0.601 → FastSign Supply 0.511 → BudgetSign Co 0.241. The **cheapest vendor ranks last** once quality and reliability are weighted in — a non-obvious, defensible conclusion.

projects.title: Field-service route optimizer — CVRP with OR-Tools
projects.summary: Quantifies what booking-order dispatch costs a small service fleet: 58.0% less driving on a synthetic 14-job, 2-van day.
projects.coverAlt: Two route maps: naive booking-order routes at 226.4 km versus OR-Tools optimized routes at 95.1 km

sections.problem: Small field-service businesses — HVAC, plumbing, electrical, sign-installation crews, couriers — dispatch vans in the order jobs were booked, not the order that minimises driving. Dispatchers rarely have a routing background, so the gap is nearly universal under ~20 vehicles.
sections.approach:
- Model the day as a **Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem** and solve it with Google **OR-Tools** (path-cheapest-arc start, guided local search).
- Compare against the naive baseline: jobs visited in booking order, split evenly across vans.
- Time-window scaffolding (`AddDimension`) is already in place for customer availability slots.
sections.result: Synthetic 14-job day, 2 vans (`--jobs 14 --vans 2 --seed 7`): **226.4 km → 95.1 km, a 58.0% distance reduction**, ≈ $22,984/year at $0.70/km for one route per day. The chart above is plotted directly from that run of the repo code. Synthetic data is optimistic; the README notes 20–40% as the realistic range for fleets that have never route-optimised.

projects.title: Auth Service — JWT, sessions and revocation from scratch
projects.summary: Standalone auth: register/login/refresh/revoke, session tracking, token blacklist and login rate limiting, deployed on a VPS.

gallery.alt: Auth service architecture diagram
gallery.caption: Request flow: FastAPI routes → service layer → PostgreSQL (users, refresh tokens, sessions, blacklist).

sections.problem: Not "how to use an auth library" — the full shape of an auth system: where the trust boundaries are, what a token actually promises, and what operations look like when you own the whole stack.
sections.approach:
- Short-lived **JWT access tokens** + long-lived, DB-backed **refresh tokens** (revocable → "sign out everywhere").
- A **blacklist** for pre-expiry access-token kills on logout, with TTL cleanup.
- Sessions as first-class records (IP + user-agent) with per-device revocation.
- Login rate limit: **5 requests / IP / 5 min**.
- structlog + request-ID middleware from day one; deployed on an Oracle Cloud VPS behind nginx with TLS.
sections.result: Nine endpoints covering the whole lifecycle (`/auth/register`, `/login`, `/refresh`, `/revoke`, `/revoke-all`, `/logout`, `/me`, `/sessions`, `DELETE /sessions/{id}`). Lessons from the postmortem: every "temporary" record needs an owner for its end of life, and rate limiting behind a proxy is a trust decision on `X-Forwarded-For` — the first draft rate-limited the proxy itself.

projects.title: Job Queue — PostgreSQL-backed task queue, no Redis
projects.summary: Atomic claim with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, bounded retries and a dead-letter quarantine — a queue as a pattern, not a broker.

gallery.alt: Job queue architecture diagram
gallery.caption: Producer → jobs table → competing workers → COMPLETED or DEAD_LETTER.

sections.problem: Installing Celery takes an afternoon; explaining what it does is another matter. The goal was to build the smallest thing that is genuinely a queue — push/pop/retry, competing consumers, dead-letter handling — and let every shortcut show where the real engineering is.
sections.approach:
- The queue is a Postgres table; the claim is `SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, so competing workers never grab the same row and job state stays transactional with the business data.
- Status enum `PENDING → RUNNING → COMPLETED / DEAD_LETTER`, bounded retries (`MAX_RETRIES = 5`) with the error message written on the row.
- Dead-letter as quarantine, not deletion; structured JSON logs with request IDs.
sections.result: A queue reduced to four parts you can write down: **atomic claim + status column + retry policy + dead-letter quarantine**. The postmortem names the next fixes honestly — short claim transaction with a lease heartbeat, exponential backoff with jitter, `LISTEN/NOTIFY` instead of a 2-second busy poll.

projects.title: plotpoint.space — Letterboxd-powered multiplayer film party game
projects.summary: Jackbox-style game: friends connect Letterboxd accounts and guess who picked which movie, live over WebSockets. Archived.
projects.coverAlt: Plot Point UI/UX flow overview showing the app's four main tabs

gallery.alt: UI/UX flow overview
gallery.caption: UI/UX flow: Discover, Play, Collections, Studio.

gallery.alt: Desktop landing screen
gallery.caption: Web landing with Google sign-in.

sections.problem: Film nights with friends need a game that uses what people actually watch. Letterboxd already holds everyone's movie history — the question was whether that data could drive a real-time party game that runs on iOS, Android and web from one codebase.
sections.approach:
- **FastAPI** backend with WebSocket rooms; a host creates a game and shares a 6-letter code, minimum 3 players.
- Each player enters a Letterboxd username; rounds show a film from someone's list and everyone guesses whose it is, with a 15-second voting timer and auto-reveal.
- **React Native (Expo)** universal client, Zustand state with AsyncStorage persistence.
sections.result: A working cross-platform multiplayer game with live rounds, scoring and end-of-game awards (Best Guesser, Most Mysterious). The product is now **archived** and the source repository is private.
